items.title: [Bug] DFlash target_layer_ids fallback guesses wrong tap layers; count collision fails silently
items.body:
## Describe the bug

`DFlashDraftConfig.resolve_target_layer_ids` (`python/sglang/srt/speculative/dflash_utils.py`) falls back to `build_target_layer_ids` when the draft config omits `dflash_config.target_layer_ids`. That fallback can never be correct, and in one case it fails silently:

1. The tap list is a training-time choice baked into the checkpoint: it determines `fc`'s input width and which target layers the drafter was trained to read. It cannot be recomputed at load time.
2. The reference repo surveyed all 20 published z-lab DFlash/DFlash2 checkpoints (z-lab/dflash#156): every one sets `dflash_config.target_layer_ids`, so the fallback is dead code today, and the formula's guess would be wrong for 14 of 20 if it ever ran.
3. The dangerous failure mode is a count collision. For `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` the formula produces the right number of taps but different layer ids (`[1, 16, 31, 46, 61]` vs the trained `[5, 19, 33, 47, 61]`). Weights load cleanly, nothing errors, and the draft silently reads the wrong target layers, which collapses acceptance. A config missing the key (hand-written config, future checkpoint format change) would hit this with no diagnostic.

The reference implementation is removing the same helper and making the key required (z-lab/dflash#156, z-lab/dflash#157).

## Reproduction

Load any DFlash draft config without `dflash_config.target_layer_ids`: `resolve_target_layer_ids` returns formula-guessed ids instead of failing. If the guessed count matches the checkpoint's `fc` width, the model runs with silently wrong context features.

## Environment

Code inspection against current main; the fallback is reachable from both `resolve_target_layer_ids` call sites (`spec_aux_hidden_state.py`, `models/dflash.py`).

I have a fix ready (require the key with a clear error, delete the helper, add CPU regression tests) and will open the PR referencing this issue.

items.title: [RFC] Aggressive test cleanup: delete tests that cannot fail, and make the directory encode the CI contract
items.body:
# Summary

Test code has grown 10.8x in twelve months. `test/` went from 46,581 lines / 228 files to **504,833 lines / 2,123 files**, with **+112,547 lines in August 2026 alone**. A second test tree lives inside the package at `python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/` — **73,054 lines across 252 files**, of which +29,490 lines arrived in August. Much of the recent growth on both sides is agent-generated, and a measurable fraction of it asserts nothing that any future diff could break.

This RFC proposes an aggressive cleanup in three PRs, deletion first, plus a structural change that keeps the growth from coming back:

**1. Delete the tests that cannot fail for a real reason.** Mock-driven mirror tests, tests that assert only that a call happened, and tests whose only coupling to SGLang is the mock they patched.

**2. Make the directory encode the CI contract, and the registration encode the hardware.**

```text
test/registered/<kind>/<subsystem>/test_*.py
```

`<kind>` ∈ `unit` / `kernel` / `e2e` / `accuracy` / `perf` / `stress`. Hardware coverage is expressed only by `register_{cuda,amd,npu,xpu,mlx}_ci(...)` on the same file — never by copying the file into a per-hardware directory.

**3. Fold the diffusion test tree into the same framework.** It currently has its own 694-line `run_suite.py`, its own suite tables, no `register_*_ci` markers, and therefore no coverage from `check_registered_tests.py`, `compute_partitions.py`, or the admission rule.

Today none of these axes are structural. `test/registered/` has 66 sibling directories mixing test kind (`unit`, `perf`, `stress`, `models_e2e`), subsystem (`attention`, `moe`, `spec`, `mem_cache`) and hardware (`amd`, `npu`, `xpu`, `musa`, `mlx`, `cpu`, `gb300`) at one level, and diffusion sits outside all of it. That flatness is why **110 device-hours of per-PR CI time goes to perf/accuracy tests most PRs cannot affect**, why **70 files are byte-structure duplicates of each other**, and why the admission criteria we already agreed on have no reach into the fastest-growing part of the tree.

# Why

## The cost is not where the code is

Per-commit CI cost attributed back to source: every `register_*_ci()` parsed via AST, filtered against `PER_COMMIT_SUITES` in `test/run_suite.py`, multiplied by the device count in the suite name. Grouped by test *kind* rather than by directory:

| kind | files | LOC | % of LOC | device-h per PR | % of CI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `unit` | 726 | 236,453 | 46.8% | 3.0 | 1.0% |
| `kernel` | 300 | 77,849 | 15.4% | 9.0 | 2.9% |
| `e2e` | 642 | 116,586 | 23.1% | 191.0 | 60.9% |
| `accuracy` | 104 | 17,194 | 3.4% | 31.7 | 10.1% |
| `perf` | 80 | 10,510 | 2.1% | 79.1 | 25.2% |
| `stress` | 4 | 216 | 0.0% | 0.0 | 0% |
| `manual` (unregistered) | 243 | 45,995 | 9.1% | 0.0 | 0% |

*(kind assigned by a heuristic over path + suite name + `est_time`; totals are exact, individual assignments approximate.)*

`unit` + `kernel` is 62% of the code and 3.9% of per-PR CI time. `perf` + `accuracy` is 5.5% of the code and 35.3% of it. Deleting agent-generated unit tests is worth doing on maintenance and review-bandwidth grounds — it is not a CI-cost argument, and this RFC does not make it one. The CI-cost argument is entirely about suite placement.

Per directory the inversion is sharper: `test/registered/unit/` is 38.5% of test LOC and 0.8% of per-PR device-hours (47 device-seconds per kLOC); `test/registered/npu/` is 3.4% of LOC and 41.0% of device-hours (26,911 device-seconds per kLOC).

## Tests that cannot fail for a real reason

Three AST signals, run over `test/registered/` and `python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/` together:

| signal | files | LOC | cases |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **B.** call-assertions ≥ real assertions — the test proves a function *was called*, not that anything is correct | 21 | 3,596 | 124 |
| **C.** ≥10 mock references and ≥3x as many mock refs as real `sglang.srt` / `sglang.multimodal_gen` imports | 144 | 63,722 | 2,322 |
| **screening set (B ∪ C)** | **158** | **65,044** | **2,363** |

That is 9% of files and 13% of lines across the two trees. It splits **119 files / 51,751 lines in `test/registered/` (12% of that tree)** and **39 files / 13,293 lines in the diffusion tree (22% of that tree)** — diffusion is proportionally about twice as affected.

Concrete shape of what the signals catch:

| file | mock refs | real asserts | call-asserts | sglang imports | cases | LOC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `unit/layers/test_minicpm_sparse_metadata.py` | 177 | 100 | 16 | 8 | 31 | 1,462 |
| `unit/managers/test_generation_auxiliary_output.py` | 111 | 36 | 23 | 9 | 25 | 732 |
| `unit/platforms/test_platform_interface.py` | 102 | 85 | 21 | 12 | 60 | 804 |
| `multimodal_gen/test/unit/test_component_residency.py` | 60 | 0 | 19 | — | 20 | 480 |
| `unit/managers/test_priority_scheduling_disaggregation.py` | 69 | 29 | 23 | 7 | 15 | 512 |

A file with 177 mock references and 8 real imports is not testing SGLang; it is testing the mock. `unit-test-admission.md` already names this category — "mirror tests that restate the implementation logic as assertions" — and it is currently 65,044 lines of the repo.

**These signals screen; they do not auto-delete.** A fourth signal I tried — "zero real assertions" — produced 186 files, all false positives: the `attention/unittests/` families delegate their assertions to a shared harness. It is dropped. The remaining two are the candidate list for human review, exactly as #30703 handled its batch.

## Hardware-as-a-directory manufactures duplicates

Because `amd/` and `npu/` are directories rather than registrations, adding hardware coverage looks like *copying a file*. Result: **29 groups of structurally identical files, 70 redundant files, 6,088 recoverable lines** (4,040 in `registered/amd/`, 1,114 in `registered/npu/`). The most expensive group:

```
$ diff test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi30x/test_minimax_m25_eval_amd.py \
       test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi30x/test_minimax_m27_eval_amd.py
```

Two 245-line files, five differing values: model path, suite name, class name, docstring, `num_questions`. Five files in that group, five more in the sibling `grok` group, four in `amd/test_deepseek_v4_*`, four in `amd/perf/mi30x/`. On the NPU side, `npu/vlm_models/` has 14 identical 26-line declaration files and `npu/llm_models/` has 8; 72 of 184 NPU files are declaration-only wrappers over a shared base class.

## Nothing structural keeps a perf test off the per-commit path

Perf tests live in `registered/npu/performance/`, `registered/amd/perf/`, `registered/perf/`, and inline in subsystem directories. Registered to per-commit suites today:

| file | suite | est_time | devices | device-h / PR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `npu/performance/qwen3_5_397b/test_npu_qwen3_5_397b_w4a8_8p_in3k5_out1k5_50ms.py` | `base-c-test-perf-16-npu-a3` | 3600 | 16 | 16.0 |
| `npu/performance/qwen3_235b_a22b/test_npu_qwen3_235b_w8a8_8p_in3k5_out1k5_50ms.py` | `base-c-test-perf-16-npu-a3` | 3600 | 16 | 16.0 |
| `npu/accuracy/glm5_top64_pruned/test_npu_glm5_top64_pruned_bf16_8p_gsm8k.py` | `base-c-test-acc-16-npu-a3` | 3600 | 16 | 16.0 |
| `amd/perf/mi35x/test_qwen35_fp8_ar_fusion_mi35x.py` | `stage-c-test-large-8-gpu-amd-mi35x` | 4800 | 8 | 10.7 |
| `amd/test_moriep_small.py` | `stage-c-test-large-8-gpu-amd` | 5400 | 8 | 12.0 |

The filename already declares the contract — `in3k5_out1k5_50ms` is a TPOT SLA. The directory does not, so the suite tag is the only thing between a benchmark and every contributor's PR, and it is one keyword argument.

Related: there are **208 distinct suite names, 110 of which contain exactly one file**. A single-file suite gets nothing from `auto_partition`'s LPT balancing while still paying a full runner acquisition, install, and warmup.

## The diffusion tree is outside every guardrail

`python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/` is 252 files and 73,054 lines, grown from 22,074 lines in June. It has:

- its own `run_suite.py` (694 lines) with its own `SUITES` / `FILE_SUITES` / `STRICT_SUITES` / `COMPONENT_ACCURACY_SUITES` tables and a hand-maintained `STANDALONE_FILE_EST_TIMES` dict;
- **zero `register_*_ci` markers**, so `scripts/lint/check_registered_tests.py` (hooked on `^test/registered/.*\.py$`) and `compute_partitions.py` (globs `test/registered/**`) do not see it;
- no reach from `.claude/rules/unit-test-admission.md`, which is scoped to `test/**/*.py`;
- its own workflow, `pr-test-multimodal-gen.yml`.

Two test frameworks in one repo means every guardrail has to be built twice, and in practice the second one never gets built. That is the most likely explanation for why the diffusion tree carries 22% mock-driven tests against `test/registered/`'s 12%.

## File count, not line count, drives the CPU gate

Measured per-file timings from [`sglang-ci-stats/model.json`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sgl-project/sglang-ci-stats/main/model.json) (n_runs=14, 7-day window). `base-a-test-cpu` is 547 files / 6,537s = **109 minutes**:

```
  0-4   s:    2 files
  5-9   s:   76 files  ############
  10-11 s:  317 files  ####################################################
  12-14 s:  113 files  ##################
  15-19 s:   14 files
  20-29 s:   13 files
  30+   s:   12 files
             min=0  p10=7  median=11  p90=13  max=158
```

317 files pile into one 10–11s bucket. That is a fixed-cost floor, not a distribution of test work: `run_unittest_files` launches each file as its own `python3 file.py -f` subprocess, so every file pays `import torch` + `import sglang` again. At p10=7s that is 3,829 of the 6,537 seconds — **59% of the suite is process startup**. `base-a-test-cpu` gates every GPU stage through `wait-for-base-a`, so this is serial latency on the critical path of every PR.

## And the growth is self-reinforcing

`_pr-test-check-changes.yml`'s `main_package` paths-filter includes `"test/**/!(*.md)"`. Any test-file change triggers the full main_package suite set, including the 128.7 NPU device-hours. Adding tests makes CI slower for everyone who adds tests.

# Proposed Shape

## Target layout

```text
test/
  registered/                 # CI-registered; run_suite.py globs registered/**/*.py
    unit/                     # no server, no engine, no GPU  -> base-a-test-cpu
      <subsystem>/
    kernel/                   # single-operator correctness + microbench -> base-b-kernel-*
      <group>/                # mirrors sglang.kernels.ops.<group> (RFC #29630)
    e2e/                      # launches a server/engine; small models; per-commit
      <subsystem>/            # ... including diffusion/
    accuracy/                 # eval floors (gsm8k / mmlu / mmmu) on real models -> nightly
      <model-family>/
    perf/                     # throughput / latency SLA -> nightly
      <model-family>/
    stress/                   # long-running soak -> weekly
  manual/                     # not CI-registered
  lm_eval_configs/            # unchanged
```

Inserting a `<kind>/` level is transparent to existing tooling: `compute_partitions.discover_files()` globs `test/registered/**/*.py` recursively, `run_suite.py` does the same, and the `check-registered-tests` pre-commit hook matches `^test/registered/.*\.py$`. No workflow, partitioner, or lint hook needs to know the new level exists.

## Hardware becomes a registration, not a directory

`registered/{amd,npu,xpu,musa,mlx,cpu,gb300}/` are dissolved. A scenario lives once, in its `<kind>/<subsystem>/` home, and declares every backend that runs it:

```python
# test/registered/accuracy/minimax/test_minimax_eval.py
register_cuda_ci(est_time=900, stage="base-c", runner_config="8-gpu-h200", nightly=True)
register_amd_ci(est_time=980, suite="nightly-amd-accuracy-8-gpu-minimax", nightly=True)
```

Hardware-specific scenarios do not disappear — a ROCm-only aiter path or an Ascend-only graph mode is a file that registers only that backend. What goes away is the copy: one scenario, one file, N registrations. For model matrices the file carries a table instead of being duplicated per model, which is also what makes future subset selection possible: 14 separate files cannot be filtered by what a PR touched, one table can.

## Kind determines the suite, and lint enforces it

Extending `scripts/lint/check_registered_tests.py` — already hooked on the right path, already AST-only, already has its own unit tests under `scripts/lint/test_check_*.py`:

| kind | allowed suites | additional constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `unit` | CPU suites only | no `popen_launch_server`; no GPU registration; `est_time <= 60` |
| `kernel` | `*-kernel-*` | — |
| `e2e` | per-commit `base-*` / `stage-*` | `est_time <= 900` |
| `accuracy` | `nightly-*` / `weekly-*` | `nightly=True` required |
| `perf` | `nightly-*` / `weekly-*` | `nightly=True` required |
| `stress` | `stress` / `weekly-*` | — |

A perf test can then no longer reach the per-commit path by accident: it becomes a lint failure rather than something review has to catch.

## Two gaps in the admission criteria

[`.claude/rules/unit-test-admission.md`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.claude/rules/unit-test-admission.md) already answers "should this case exist". Two things it does not cover, both of which the data above argues for:

1. **File granularity.** The rule says nothing about whether a new case warrants a new *file*, yet file count is what drives the CPU gate. New cases should join an existing file in the same directory by default.
2. **Suite placement.** The rule governs whether a case exists, not whether it runs per-commit or nightly — which is where the 110 device-hours went. Proposed addition: *if a failing run cannot be traced back to a single PR's diff, the case belongs in nightly.*

Its `paths:` scope also needs to reach the diffusion tree, which PR 3 fixes structurally by moving those tests under `test/registered/`.

There is a live tension worth settling in this thread: [`.claude/skills/write-sglang-test/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.claude/skills/write-sglang-test/SKILL.md) Core Rule 5 says *"Prefer mock over real server … use `unittest.mock.patch` / `MagicMock` and place tests in `test/registered/unit/`"* (#21119, 2026-03). The 65,044-line screening set above is the direct product of following that instruction literally. The skill fires when an agent *writes* a test; the rule fires on path match. Updating one without the other will not change what gets written.

# Migration Plan

Three PRs, deletion first, each independently revertable.

## PR 1 — delete

No moves, no renames. Deletions plus the occasional shrink of a surviving file, so the diff is a file list and `git log --follow` stays intact for PR 3.

- **The screening set: 158 files, 65,044 lines, 2,363 cases**, across `test/registered/` (119 files) and `python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/` (39 files). Reviewed in batches by subtree; each batch's PR description names, per file, the regression that would escape if it were deleted — the same question `unit-test-admission.md` makes authors answer, applied in reverse.
- **`test/manual/` triage.** 243 files, 45,995 lines, zero CI registration, so nothing here has ever gated a merge. Repro recipes worth keeping move to `docs/` or the relevant cookbook; the rest goes.
- Anything the screening set misses but review catches while it is in there — the point of this PR is to be aggressive while the whole tree is under one set of eyes.

The screening script and its per-file CSV ship with this PR so the list can be re-run and disputed file by file.

## PR 2 — dedup and re-tag

Structural cleanup that removes code without removing coverage, plus the suite corrections.

- Collapse the **29 structurally identical file groups → 70 files, 6,088 lines** into table-driven files with per-backend registrations (`amd/accuracy/mi30x/` minimax + grok, `amd/perf/mi30x/`, `amd/test_deepseek_v4_*`, `npu/vlm_models/`, `npu/llm_models/`, `manual/dsv4/`).
- Merge the **72 declaration-only NPU files (2,987 lines)** that already share `GSM8KAscendMixin` / `TestVLMModels` / `TestNpuAccuracyTestCaseBase` into per-family tables.
- Re-tag the **132 perf / accuracy / benchmark registrations** currently on per-commit suites to nightly, recovering **~110 device-hours per PR commit**. Each family keeps a per-commit sentinel: single device, small model, wide threshold.
- Collapse the **110 single-file suite names** into their family suites so `auto_partition` can balance them.
- Granularity rule for every merge here: **one file per shard, not one file per directory.** A merged file's `est_time` becomes the sum of its matrix, and LPT degrades if one file cannot fit a shard budget.

## PR 3 — reorganize and enforce

- `git mv` only: every remaining registered test into `test/registered/<kind>/<subsystem>/`. Byte-identical contents; import rewrites only where a test imports a sibling test module.
- **Fold the diffusion tree into the same framework**: `python/sglang/multimodal_gen/test/` moves under `test/registered/`, its cases gain `register_*_ci` markers, its `STANDALONE_FILE_EST_TIMES` dict becomes in-source `est_time`, and its `run_suite.py` is retired in favor of the shared one. `pr-test-multimodal-gen.yml` keeps its own stages and runners; only the discovery and registration layer is shared.
- Extend `scripts/lint/check_registered_tests.py` with the kind ↔ suite table, plus its tests under `scripts/lint/`.
- Merge `registered/unit/` toward roughly 2–3 files per subsystem (from 547 files in `base-a-test-cpu`). At the measured 7s floor this is worth a large share of the 109-minute critical-path gate with zero assertions deleted; the target is not one file per directory, because merging trades away failure isolation.
- Narrow the `main_package` paths-filter so a change confined to `registered/unit/` no longer triggers NPU/AMD full runs.

PR 3 is the largest and can be split by subtree if reviewers prefer; PR 1 and PR 2 are prerequisites either way, since the move is much smaller once the deletions and the per-hardware directories are gone.

# Open questions

1. **Static source ratchets** — `unit` or `scripts/lint/`? #34309 moved the guidance to `scripts/lint/` and #34913 moved it back the same day. The `<kind>/` taxonomy needs this settled: a ratchet that parses source is not really a unit test, but it is also not a linter if it needs the import graph.
2. **How wide should the per-commit sentinels be?** Every perf/accuracy family losing per-commit coverage needs one, and the aggregate of those sentinels is the real floor on what PR 2 recovers.
3. **`accuracy` split by model family or by subsystem?** Model family matches how the files are written and how owners think; subsystem matches the rest of the tree.
4. **Should `kernel/` mirror `sglang.kernels.ops.<group>` exactly?** #29630 landed that namespace; a 1:1 mirror is appealing but couples two trees.
5. **`est_time` honesty.** `compute_partitions` sizes shard count as `ceil(coeff * Σest / (0.75 * timeout * 60))`, so a padded `est_time` silently buys runners. Worth a lint bound against the measured value where one exists.
6. **Does the diffusion fold-in belong in PR 3 or its own PR?** It is the one part of PR 3 that changes how a team runs its tests day to day.

---

Every number above comes from a stdlib-only AST audit of all test files in both trees plus a `curl` of `sglang-ci-stats/model.json` — no `torch`, no `sglang` import, runs on `ubuntu-latest`. NPU and AMD device-hours are in-source `est_time` rather than measured, since `update_est_time.py` scrapes only `("cuda", "cpu")`; owners should sanity-check those. The script and its per-file CSV ship with PR 1.

items.title: [Feature] [RFC] [HiCache] Out-of-process HiCache data plane with device-memory IPC
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

### Summary

I would like to discuss whether HiCache should support an **out-of-process data-plane mode**, where a local `HiCacheDaemon` runs separately from the scheduler process and accesses the scheduler's GPU KV pool through a device-memory IPC mechanism (**CUDA IPC on NVIDIA as the initial backend**).

A key design question is where the authoritative cache metadata boundary should live. For a minimal prototype, keeping `UnifiedRadixCache` / TreeCore scheduler-local may reduce scheduler-path IPC and narrow the correctness surface, while daemon-owned TreeCore could eventually enable a single authoritative cache index across multiple schedulers.

This RFC focuses first on the out-of-process data plane and the ownership boundary around it.

A conservative initial split could look like:

```text
Scheduler process
  ├── request scheduling
  ├── UnifiedRadixCache / TreeCore
  ├── prefix matching
  ├── lock / reference semantics
  ├── GPU KV page allocation
  └── decides backup / restore intents
              │
              │ device-memory IPC + lightweight control messages
              │ (CUDA IPC initially on NVIDIA)
              ▼
HiCacheDaemon
  ├── imported GPU KV mappings
  ├── GPU <-> Host transfers
  ├── host KV cache / physical residency
  ├── asynchronous transfer queues
  ├── prefetch / backup execution
  ├── write-back / write-through execution
  └── external L3 storage clients
```

This would make HiCache's lower-tier cache and transfer path independently deployable while keeping scheduler-critical cache semantics local in the initial design.

This RFC is primarily about the **process and ownership boundary**. It is not a claim that the proposed architecture is necessarily faster than the current in-process implementation.

### Why consider this?

Today, HiCache transfer and lower-tier cache management are closely coupled to the scheduler process.

That has some potential drawbacks:

1. **Scheduler complexity**

   GPU/host transfers, asynchronous backup/load-back, storage I/O, transfer queues, and lower-tier cache lifecycle add concurrency and I/O state to the scheduler process.

2. **Failure and lifecycle coupling**

   A scheduler restart also tears down its HiCache runtime state, transfer workers, storage connections, and pending operations.

3. **Independent evolution**

   A standalone data plane could evolve, be profiled, restarted, and instrumented independently from request scheduling.

4. **Transfer resource management**

   A daemon could centrally own device transfer streams, pinned host memory, batching, throttling, storage connections, and I/O observability.

5. **Bulk KV data does not need to cross an RPC boundary**

   With device-memory IPC, the daemon can map the scheduler's existing GPU KV allocations. Normal operations can carry page IDs, offsets, keys, and synchronization handles instead of serialized tensors.

LMCache's multiprocess mode provides a useful reference point here: LMCache can run as a standalone service, and its multiprocess connector supports a device-handle path where the cache service operates on engine KV buffers through device IPC (CUDA IPC on NVIDIA).

LMCache also already contains an SGLang multiprocess adapter that communicates with a standalone LMCache daemon, so this process model is relevant to SGLang integration today as well.

### Proposed boundary

One key design question is whether TreeCore should remain scheduler-local or become daemon-owned.

For a minimal prototype, keeping TreeCore local has a useful property: operations such as

```text
match_prefix()
insert()
inc_lock_ref()
dec_lock_ref()
scheduler cache admission decisions
```

would not require daemon IPC, and the scheduler could remain authoritative for request-visible cache semantics.

The daemon would instead execute data movement and lower-tier residency operations.

Conceptually:

```text
                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
                      │      Scheduler           │
                      │                          │
request ─────────────►│  UnifiedRadixCache       │
                      │        │                 │
                      │        ▼                 │
                      │     TreeCore             │
                      │        │                 │
                      │        ▼                 │
                      │  GPU page IDs            │
                      │        │                 │
                      │  GPU KV Pool             │
                      └────────┼─────────────────┘
                               │
                     device-memory IPC mapping
                      (CUDA IPC initially)
                               │
                               ▼
                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
                      │     HiCacheDaemon        │
                      │                          │
                      │  Transfer Engine         │
                      │   ├─ D2H                 │
                      │   ├─ H2D                 │
                      │   ├─ backup              │
                      │   └─ restore             │
                      │                          │
                      │  Host KV tier            │
                      │        │                 │
                      │        ▼                 │
                      │  External L3             │
                      └──────────────────────────┘
```

This avoids putting `match_prefix()` or other scheduler hot-path tree operations behind RPC in the initial version. However, daemon-owned TreeCore remains an interesting direction if the goal expands toward authoritative cross-scheduler cache sharing.

### Device IPC data path

At initialization, a scheduler could register its GPU KV allocations with the daemon:

```text
REGISTER_KV_POOL(
    instance_id,
    generation,
    device_id,
    layout,
    memory_ipc_handles
)
```

The daemon imports those allocations once.

Subsequent operations only need descriptors, for example:

```text
BACKUP(
    operation_id,
    source_pages,
    cache_keys,
    ready_fence
)

RESTORE(
    operation_id,
    cache_keys,
    destination_pages,
    completion_fence
)
```

For the initial NVIDIA implementation, CUDA IPC would provide the memory-sharing mechanism. The daemon would still submit the actual asynchronous D2H/H2D copies on its own CUDA streams.

The long-term architecture should ideally not require CUDA-specific semantics. Other accelerator runtimes expose analogous device-memory IPC mechanisms (for example, HIP IPC and Level Zero IPC), but the exact memory-sharing and synchronization capabilities differ by platform.

In particular, I think **device-memory sharing and cross-process synchronization should be treated as separate capabilities**:

```text
DeviceMemoryIPC
  ├── export allocation
  ├── import allocation
  └── close mapping

DeviceSyncIPC
  ├── export fence/event (when supported)
  ├── import fence/event
  └── wait/query
```

A platform may have a usable memory IPC path without an equally reliable or available event-IPC path. In that case, the data plane should be able to select another completion mechanism rather than assuming CUDA-event semantics are universal.

Device IPC itself is probably not the main architectural challenge here. The harder question is how to split authoritative ownership of GPU pages, host residency, transfer completion, eviction, and failure recovery across the scheduler/daemon boundary.

For the control and completion path, possible implementations include:

* UDS / lightweight RPC;
* shared-memory submission/completion rings;
* eventfd + shared queues;
* platform-specific device event IPC when available;
* another explicit host/device synchronization mechanism as a fallback.

A high-frequency path may eventually benefit from an NVMe-style submission/completion queue, but I do not think the exact transport needs to be decided before agreeing on the ownership model.

### Ownership

A conservative first version could use the following ownership model:

```text
Scheduler owns:
- GPU KV allocation
- GPU page allocator
- TreeCore / radix metadata
- request references and locks
- GPU-page execution lifetime
- backup / restore decisions

HiCacheDaemon owns:
- imported device-memory IPC mappings
- transfer streams
- host KV physical allocation
- pending transfer state
- transfer scheduling / batching
- L3 storage clients
- lower-tier I/O metrics
```

In this model, the scheduler explicitly publishes source pages that are safe to back up and explicitly provides destination pages for restore.

This avoids introducing a cross-process GPU page allocator in the first version.

There is an important design question around **host-tier eviction metadata**: if TreeCore remains authoritative for cache semantics while the daemon owns physical host residency, eviction and invalidation need an explicit protocol so that neither side can observe stale residency.

That seems worth discussing before choosing the exact API.

### Failure and lifecycle handling

I think lifecycle handling should be treated as a first-class part of the design.

Each scheduler registration likely needs at least:

```text
instance_id
process identity
pool generation
device identity
```

If a scheduler exits or crashes, the daemon must eventually release:

* imported device-memory IPC mappings;
* imported synchronization objects;
* pending operations;
* scheduler-specific physical residency state.

A restarted scheduler must not consume completions or page references belonging to an older generation.

Likewise, daemon failure should ideally fail closed without corrupting scheduler-local GPU cache state.

For example, a possible degraded mode could be:

```text
HiCacheDaemon unavailable
        ↓
temporarily disable L2/L3 backup/load
        ↓
continue inference with scheduler-local L1 cache
```

Whether preserving host-cache contents across scheduler restarts is safe or useful could be considered separately.

### Relationship to existing SGLang work

This seems complementary to several recent SGLang efforts.

#### #24542 — standalone HiCache L3 StorageServer

#24542 proposed a standalone storage process using UDS/gRPC for control and shared `memfd` host memory for the bulk data path.

Its central principle is similar:

```text
control plane -> descriptors
data plane    -> shared memory
```

This RFC asks whether that process boundary could move one tier closer to the accelerator:

```text
#24542

SGLang HiCache
    │
shared host memory
    ▼
Standalone L3 StorageServer


This proposal

SGLang scheduler
    │
device-memory IPC
(CUDA IPC initially)
    ▼
HiCacheDaemon
    ├── Host tier
    └── L3 storage
```

#### #32710 — Rust TreeCore

The merged Rust TreeCore work makes the tree/data-plane boundary more explicit.

One possible architecture is:

```text
Scheduler
    ├── scheduling
    ├── Rust TreeCore
    └── GPU allocator
             │
      device-memory IPC
       (CUDA initially)
             │
             ▼
       HiCacheDaemon
             ├── transfer engine
             ├── host tier
             └── external storage
```

This could keep the latency-sensitive metadata path in-process while moving bulk cache operations out of the scheduler. A future daemon-owned TreeCore design could be considered separately if cross-scheduler authoritative metadata becomes a goal.

#### #35648 — shared KV pool with CUDA IPC

#35648 explores cross-process KV sharing with a CUDA-IPC-visible physical KV allocation.

Although its goal is different (same-GPU model replicas), it highlights many of the same systems questions:

* ownership;
* publication;
* generations;
* reference lifetime;
* synchronization;
* failure recovery.

This proposal focuses specifically on the HiCache transfer/data plane rather than cross-scheduler shared prefix ownership.

### TreeCore placement

There are at least two plausible designs:

```text
A. Scheduler-local TreeCore

Scheduler
├── TreeCore
├── GPU allocator
└── execution
       │
       ▼
HiCacheDaemon
├── host tier
├── transfer
└── L3
```

This minimizes scheduler-path IPC and keeps request/cache coordination in one process.

A more aggressive design is:

```text
B. Daemon-owned TreeCore

Scheduler A ─┐
Scheduler B ─┼──► HiCacheDaemon
Scheduler C ─┘      ├── TreeCore
                    ├── cache directory
                    ├── residency
                    └── transfer
```

This could provide a single authoritative cache index across multiple schedulers, but it would also move prefix matching, locking, insertion, and potentially eviction decisions across an IPC boundary and turn more of request/cache coordination into a distributed state machine.

For a first experiment, scheduler-local TreeCore seems like the smaller correctness surface. I would still like maintainer feedback on whether that is the right long-term boundary.

### Potential benefits

If this architecture works well, possible benefits include:

* less cache I/O and transfer concurrency inside scheduler processes;
* independent HiCache lifecycle and observability;
* centralized transfer batching and bandwidth control;
* cleaner storage-backend integration;
* easier experimentation with alternative data-plane implementations;
* isolation of storage or transfer failures from scheduler logic;
* a clearer separation between cache semantics and cache movement;
* potentially reusable local cache infrastructure across inference processes.

### Costs and risks

There are also meaningful costs:

* IPC/control-message overhead;
* device-memory IPC mapping and synchronization lifecycle complexity;
* harder crash cleanup;
* host-residency metadata synchronization;
* daemon accelerator-context overhead;
* additional deployment complexity;
* possible synchronization stalls if the protocol is poorly designed;
* hardware/platform differences in memory IPC and inter-process event support.

LMCache MP's experience also suggests that stale IPC mappings, worker death, event lifetime, and cleanup behavior need explicit design and testing rather than being treated as edge cases.

### Possible minimal prototype

Instead of moving all HiCache functionality at once, a useful first experiment might only support:

* NVIDIA CUDA / Linux;
* one scheduler process;
* one local daemon;
* one GPU;
* Full attention only;
* GPU <-> host backup and restore;
* CUDA IPC as the initial device-memory IPC backend;
* scheduler-owned GPU allocator;
* scheduler-local TreeCore;
* no external L3 initially.

The goal would be to compare:

```text
current in-process HiCache transfer path

vs.

scheduler
   │
CUDA IPC
   ▼
standalone HiCacheDaemon
```

while keeping cache semantics unchanged.

Useful measurements would include:

* TTFT;
* ITL impact;
* backup/load latency;
* scheduler CPU time;
* transfer throughput;
* overlap with model execution;
* IPC/control overhead;
* GPU/host memory overhead;
* behavior under scheduler and daemon failure.

### Questions for maintainers

I would especially appreciate feedback on the following:

1. Does an out-of-process HiCache **data plane** look like a useful architectural direction for SGLang?

2. Should `UnifiedRadixCache` / TreeCore remain scheduler-local initially, or should daemon-owned TreeCore be considered from the start?

3. Should the scheduler continue to own the GPU KV allocator, with the daemon only importing its allocations through a device-memory IPC backend (CUDA IPC on NVIDIA initially)?

4. Should the host KV pool and host-tier allocator move into the daemon, or remain scheduler-owned initially?

5. What should be authoritative for host-tier residency / eviction metadata?

6. Should device-memory sharing and cross-process synchronization be modeled as separate platform capabilities, rather than assuming CUDA IPC + CUDA event IPC semantics?

7. Should one daemon serve one scheduler, one GPU, or potentially multiple scheduler processes on the same node?

8. Would an NVIDIA GPU <-> host-only prototype be a useful first step before integrating other device IPC backends and existing HiCache L3 backends?

The intent of this RFC is to discuss the **process boundary, ownership model, portability boundary, and failure semantics first**, rather than proposing an immediate large HiCache refactor.

---

### Related resources

* SGLang #24542 — `[RFC] [HiCache] A new backend for external L3 storage systems`
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/24542

* SGLang #32710 — `[Radix Cache] Add Rust TreeCore backend with shared parity tests`
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32710

* SGLang #35648 — `[Feature] [RFC] Same-GPU model replicas with managed CUDA MPS and a shared KV pool`
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/35648

* LMCache multiprocess mode / `LMCacheMPConnector`
  https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst

* LMCache SGLang multiprocess adapter
  https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/lmcache/integration/sglang/multi_process_adapter.py

* AMD HIP IPC APIs (`hipIpcGetMemHandle`, `hipIpcOpenMemHandle`, event IPC)
  https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/latest/doxygen/html/group___device.html

* Intel Level Zero IPC memory handles
  https://oneapi-src.github.io/level-zero-spec/level-zero/latest/core/EXT_IPC_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE.html

items.title: [Guide] Setup and Troubleshooting for SGLang on V100
items.body:
# SGLang Installation on NVIDIA V100

> **Note:** This installation attempt was performed on a GITC NVIDIA V100 by Nguyễn Ánh Dương @Duong-John.

This SGLang installation attempt was investigated from multiple GitHub bug reports. One of the most important references that helped make the installation successful was:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/831

Because the V100 uses the **sm70** architecture, some auxiliary frameworks that are normally installed together with SGLang, such as **FlashInfer**, do not support this architecture. Therefore, these dependencies and the SGLang source code need to be handled carefully.

## Tested Software Versions

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| Python | 3.10 |
| PyTorch | 2.3.1+cu121 |
| vLLM backend | 0.5.3.post1 |
| SGLang | 0.2.6 |

> **vLLM note:** vLLM is used as an alternative attention backend when FlashInfer is disabled.

---

# A. Installation

## Step 1: Install Conda, Set Up the Environment, and Install Packages

### 1.1 Install Miniconda

```bash
cd /home/u001012
mkdir -p miniconda3
wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh -O miniconda3/miniconda.sh
bash miniconda3/miniconda.sh -b -u -p /home/u001012/miniconda3
rm miniconda3/miniconda.sh
```

### 1.2 Activate Conda and Initialize Bash

```bash
source /home/u001012/miniconda3/bin/activate
conda init bash
```

> **Note:** After this step, it may be necessary to close and reopen the terminal. After reopening it, run `bash` again so that the shell prompt shows `(base)`.

### 1.3 Create the Python Environment and Install CUDA Toolkit 12.1

Create a virtual environment named `sgl`:

```bash
conda create -n sgl python=3.10 -y
conda activate sgl
```

Install CUDA Toolkit 12.1 into the Conda environment:

```bash
conda install -c "nvidia/label/cuda-12.1.1" cuda-toolkit -y
```

> **Note:** GITC does not currently have `nvcc` installed by default, nor does it necessarily provide it through an available module.

### 1.4 Install PyTorch

Install PyTorch 2.3.1 with CUDA 12.1 support:

```bash
pip install torch==2.3.1 torchvision==0.18.1 torchaudio==2.3.1 \
    --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
```

### 1.5 Install vLLM and Required Packages

```bash
pip install vllm==0.5.3.post1 requests==2.32.3 tqdm==4.66.4 \
    numpy==1.26.4 aiohttp==3.9.5 fastapi==0.111.1 uvicorn==0.30.3
```

### 1.6 Clone SGLang and Checkout Version 0.2.6

```bash
mkdir -p /home/u001012/Spe_Pro
cd /home/u001012/Spe_Pro
git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang.git
cd sglang
git checkout v0.2.6
```

---

## 1.7 Patch `server_args.py`

Edit the SGLang source:

```bash
nano python/sglang/srt/server_args.py
```

Find the section containing `parser.add_argument(...)` inside `add_cli_args()` and add the following arguments:

```python
parser.add_argument(
    "--disable-flashinfer",
    action="store_true",
    help="Disable flashinfer attention kernels.",
)

parser.add_argument(
    "--disable-flashinfer-sampling",
    action="store_true",
    help="Disable flashinfer sampling kernels.",
)
```

### 1.8 Install the Patched SGLang Source

```bash
cd /home/u001012/Spe_Pro/sglang/python
pip install -e .
```

> **Note:** `pip install -e .` installs SGLang in editable mode. This allows the SGLang source code to be modified later without rebuilding/reinstalling the package from scratch.

---

# Step 2: Fix Errors Encountered When Starting SGLang

## 2.1 `pyairports` Package Issue

The SGLang version used here still imports `pyairports`. Newer SGLang versions appear to have removed this dependency.

The `pyairports` version currently available online is `0.0.1`. After installing it, checking:

```text
/home/u001012/miniconda3/envs/sgl/lib/python3.10/site-packages
```

may show only:

```text
pyairports-0.0.1.dist-info/
```

Normally, installing a package such as `ABC` creates both:

```text
ABC/
ABC-<version>.dist-info/
```

Here, the actual `pyairports` package directory is missing even though `pip install` does not report an error. This suggests that the package contents may have been removed or are incomplete.

### Workaround

```bash
cd /home/u001012/miniconda3/envs/sgl/lib/python3.10/site-packages/
mkdir pyairports
touch pyairports/__init__.py
echo "AIRPORT_LIST = []" > pyairports/airports.py
```

> **Note:** `__init__.py` tells Python that `pyairports` is a valid module/package. The `airports.py` file provides a dummy `AIRPORT_LIST` variable that `outlines` attempts to import.

---

## 2.2 `transformers` Version Issue

With the current environment, `transformers` versions newer than `4.43.2` cause compatibility problems. The newer versions require PyTorch >= 2.5, while this setup uses PyTorch 2.3.1.

Install the compatible version:

```bash
pip install transformers==4.43.2
```

---

## 2.3 `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flashinfer'`

The V100 uses the **sm70** architecture, which is not supported by FlashInfer in this setup.

Although the following flags prevent SGLang from actually using FlashInfer:

```text
--disable-flashinfer
--disable-flashinfer-sampling
```

the SGLang source still imports `flashinfer` at the beginning of `infer_batch.py`.

Therefore, FlashInfer still needs to be installed so that Python can resolve the import. It is not expected to be used at runtime because the disable flags prevent SGLang from invoking it.

Install the required package:

```bash
pip install flashinfer==0.1.2+cu121torch2.3 \
    --extra-index-url https://flashinfer.ai/whl/cu121/torch2.3/
```

---

## 2.4 `RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'MainThread'`

This is a Python compatibility issue related to asynchronous processing with `asyncio` and `uvloop`.

When SGLang v0.2.6 initializes the detokenizer process, the following line in `detokenizer_manager.py` may fail:

```python
loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
```

On Python 3.10+, `asyncio.get_event_loop()` is stricter and can throw an exception when no event loop has been created.

### Workaround

Replace the line with:

```python
try:
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
except RuntimeError:
    loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()
    asyncio.set_event_loop(loop)
```

---

# B. Garbage / Meaningless Output When Running Models Larger Than 0.5B

This issue was discovered while comparing:

- `models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`
- `models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct`

The `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` model produced reasonable output corresponding to the input.

In contrast, `Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct` produced garbage output, mixed languages, hallucinated/self-generated content unrelated to the input, or sometimes returned nothing at all, even though the underlying SGLang server reported no errors.

## Possible Causes

### Cause 1: Multi-Head Attention and `head_dim`

The suspected issue is related to the attention head dimension.

The `0.5B` model uses:

```text
head_dim = 64
```

while the `7B` and `14B` models use:

```text
head_dim = 128
```

The head dimension can be calculated as:

```text
head_dim = hidden_size / num_attention_heads
```

The V100 uses the **sm70** architecture and has approximately **96 KB of shared memory per SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)**.

For example:

```text
Qwen 0.5B:
head_dim = 64
896 / 14 = 64
```

A Triton kernel may be able to tile the computation into the 96 KB SRAM available on the V100.

For Qwen 7B and 14B:

```text
head_dim = 128
4096 / 32 = 128
```

The required allocation may exceed the available 96 KB, potentially causing an overflow and resulting in corrupted attention matrices.

> **Important:** This explanation is a hypothesis from the original note, not a confirmed root cause.

### Cause 2: Older Triton Matrix Tiling

Another possible cause is that the older Triton compiler does not correctly tile a matrix requiring approximately 96 KB of SRAM.

Newer Triton nightly builds may support this case.

This hypothesis is based on the following community report:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/54

The reported symptoms were similar to the issue observed here. The community suggested upgrading Triton to a newer nightly version.

In this setup, **Cause 2 was used as the practical solution**, because there was supporting community feedback.

---

## Fix: Upgrade Triton

```bash
pip install --upgrade triton
```

> **Note:** Warnings or installation errors may appear during the upgrade. The installed version in the final environment was typically greater than 3.0.

### Follow-up Triton Compatibility Issue

After upgrading Triton, another error may occur during:

```python
from triton.runtime.cache import ...
```

The error may mention missing symbols such as:

- `FileCacheManager`
- `default_dump_dir`
- `default_override_dir`
- `default_cache_dir`

The reason is that SGLang v0.2.6 was originally installed with a Triton 2.x version. In the SGLang `utils.py`, the code imports cache-management functions from Triton.

With Triton 3.x, these functions may have been renamed or moved, causing an `ImportError`.

Find the following code in `/home/u001012/Spe_Pro/sglang/python/sglang/srt/utils.py`:

```python
from triton.runtime.cache import (
    FileCacheManager,
    default_dump_dir,
    default_override_dir,
)
```

Replace it with:

```python
import os

try:
    from triton.runtime.cache import (
        FileCacheManager,
        default_cache_dir,
        default_dump_dir,
        default_override_dir,
    )
except ImportError:
    def default_cache_dir():
        return os.environ.get(
            "TRITON_CACHE_DIR",
            os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".triton", "cache")
        )

    def default_dump_dir():
        return os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".triton", "dump")

    def default_override_dir():
        return os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".triton", "override")

    class FileCacheManager:
        def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
            pass

        def get_file(self, *args, **kwargs):
            return None

        def put(self, *args, **kwargs):
            pass
```

---

# C. Running SGLang

## 1. Start the Server

Activate the Conda environment:

```bash
source /home/u001012/miniconda3/bin/activate sgl
```

Set the model:

```bash
MODEL_PATH="Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct"
```

Start SGLang:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path $MODEL_PATH \
    --dtype half \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --tp-size 1 \
    --disable-flashinfer \
    --disable-flashinfer-sampling \
    --disable-cuda-graph \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.92
```

### Important Runtime Options

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--model-path` | Model to load |
| `--dtype half` | Use FP16 |
| `--trust-remote-code` | Allow model-provided remote code |
| `--tp-size 1` | Use one tensor-parallel rank |
| `--disable-flashinfer` | Disable FlashInfer attention kernels |
| `--disable-flashinfer-sampling` | Disable FlashInfer sampling kernels |
| `--disable-cuda-graph` | Disable CUDA Graph |
| `--mem-fraction-static 0.92` | Allocate 92% of GPU memory for static memory |

---

# 2. Send a Request from the Client

Example prompt:

```python
prompt = (
    "<|im_start|>system\n"
    "You are an expert programming assistant who explains things concisely and directly."
    "<|im_end|>\n"
    "<|im_start|>user\n"
    "Write a C++ CUDA kernel function for matrix multiplication."
    "<|im_end|>\n"
    "<|im_start|>assistant\n"
)
```

Request data:

```python
data = {
    "text": prompt,
    "sampling_params": {
        "temperature": 0.0,
        "max_new_tokens": 1000,
        "stop": ["<|im_end|>", "<|endoftext|>"]
    }
}
```

---

# 3. Execution and Results

The server was queried twice to verify that the server was running correctly and that **Cache Hit** from the **RadixAttention** tree was working.

Example model output:

```cpp
__global__ void matrixMulKernel(float* A, float* B, float* C, int Width) {
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

    if (row < Width && col < Width) {
        float sum = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < Width; k++) {
            sum += A[row * Width + k] * B[k * Width + col];
        }
        C[row * Width + col] = sum;
    }
}
```

The model explained that:

- `A`, `B`, and `C` are the input and output matrices.
- `Width` is the dimension of the square matrices.
- `blockDim` and `gridDim` divide the work among threads and blocks.
- Each thread computes one element of the output matrix `C`.

To use this kernel, data must be transferred from the host (CPU) to the device (GPU), the kernel must be launched, and the resulting data must then be transferred back from the device to the host.

### Example Client Output

```text
Response latency: 12.36 seconds

(sgl) [u001012@gpunode1 Spe_Pro]$ python client.py
Sending raw request to SGLang server...

=== MODEL OUTPUT ===
```

The second request produced the same matrix-multiplication kernel output, demonstrating that the request was processed consistently.

---

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 fails to load on v0.5.17/v0.5.18: AssertionError: Hidden size mismatch in the mxfp4 MoE path (works on main)
items.body:
> **Corrected 2026-09-01** — the original report claimed two defects (fp8 experts misdetected as fp4, plus an fp8-loader shape mismatch). Both claims were wrong and I have removed them; see the comment below. Auto-detection is correct, and the shape error was self-inflicted by my own env override. One real defect remains, described here.

### Summary

`DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` fails to load on tagged releases **v0.5.17** and **v0.5.18** with `AssertionError: Hidden size mismatch` while loading routed-expert weights through the `flashinfer_mxfp4` MoE runner. The same checkpoint, same flags, same hardware loads and serves correctly on `main` (2026-08-30 snapshot `a1fe4e30`, verified both as a pip overlay of `python/` and via `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20260830-a1fe4e30`). It looks like the fix exists on `main` but is not in any tagged release.

### Checkpoint layout (for context)

This checkpoint is **hybrid-quantized**, which is relevant to the code path taken:

| Component | dtype in safetensors |
|---|---|
| Attention / dense layers | `F8_E4M3` weights + `F8_E8M0` scales |
| **Routed experts** | **`I8` weights** (`layers.N.ffn.experts.M.w1.weight`, e.g. shape `[2048, 2048]`) **+ `F8_E8M0` scales** (`[2048, 128]`) — mxfp4-packed |

`config.json` declares only `{"quant_method": "fp8", "fmt": "e4m3", "scale_fmt": "ue8m0", "weight_block_size": [128,128]}` — it does *not* announce the mxfp4 experts, so header probing is the only way to know. `try_detect_fp4_experts()` probes the header and correctly returns `True` here; routing to `flashinfer_mxfp4` on SM90 is the intended behavior.

### Environment

- 4×H800 80GB (SM90), single node, TP=4
- Driver 580.173.02 / CUDA 13.0
- pypi `sglang==0.5.18` (torch 2.13.0+cu130) and `sglang==0.5.17` (torch 2.11) in clean venvs — both reproduce
- Local unmodified HF repo copy of the checkpoint

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8012 --tp 4 \
  --context-length 262144 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
  --trust-remote-code
```

### Failure

With defaults (detection `True` → `moe_runner_backend=flashinfer_mxfp4`), all TP ranks die during weight loading:

```
AssertionError: Hidden size mismatch
```

Reproduced identically on v0.5.17 and v0.5.18.

(For completeness: forcing `SGLANG_DSV4_FP4_EXPERTS=0` does *not* help and should not be used here — it pushes packed 4-bit expert weights down the fp8 path and produces `RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (4096) must match the size of tensor b (2048) at non-singleton dimension 1`, which is simply the packed/unpacked width mismatch and is expected given the override.)

### Works on main

Same node, same checkpoint, same flags on `main` @ `a1fe4e30`: loads, serves, and passes our functional battery — OpenAI-compatible requests, DSPARK active (accept length ≈2.05), prefix-cache hit rate 99.2% with `--enable-cache-report`.

### Ask

1. Could you identify which `main` commit(s) fixed the mxfp4 MoE path for this checkpoint?
2. Please consider including them in the next tagged release (0.5.19?), so this checkpoint runs from pypi without a dev-tree checkout.
3. Happy to test release candidates on this hardware.

items.title: [Bug] NEXTN/MTP draft acceptance decays to ~0 over server uptime on qwen4_exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), fully restored by a restart
items.body:
### Checklist - [ ] I searched related issues but found no solution. - [ ] The bug persists in the latest version. - [ ] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback. - [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Describe the bug # [Bug] NEXTN/MTP draft acceptance decays to ~0 over server uptime on qwen4_exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), fully restored by a restart ## Summary On `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (`qwen4_exp`, hybrid GDN linear-attention + QSA sparse full-attention MoE) served with NEXTN speculative decoding, draft acceptance is healthy at boot and **decays to near-zero over roughly 24 hours of uptime**. Throughput falls ~2.9x. There is no crash, no error, and no warning in the log — the server just gets progressively slower while reporting `accept rate: 0.00`. A full restart restores it completely and reproducibly. This is distinct from #21138 (constant 0.33 from boot, NemotronH weight-loading, fixed by #30456) and from #19796 (radix-cache prefix hit → NaN crash, not gradual decay). ## Measurements Identical prompt, `max_tokens: 400`, `temperature: 0`, single stream. | server state | accept rate | accept len | throughput | |---|---|---|---| | fresh boot | 0.47 – 0.76 | 2.4 – 3.3 | 31 – 47 tok/s (74.5 peak logged) | | after ~4 days uptime | 0.00 – 0.20 | 1.00 – 1.60 | 16.4 – 19.6 tok/s | | after restart (same box, same args) | 0.48 – 0.74 | 2.45 – 3.23 | 40.6 – 47.1 tok/s | Decode log at boot: ``` Decode batch, #running-req: 1, ..., accept len: 3.27, accept rate: 0.76, ..., gen throughput (token/s): 31.40 ``` Decode log after ~4 days: ``` Decode batch, #running-req: 1, ..., accept len: 1.00, accept rate: 0.00, ..., gen throughput (token/s): 13.78 ``` Onset: booted 08-27, first `accept rate: 0.00` batches appear 08-28 (~24 h). Zeros then interleave with occasional low non-zeros (0.05–0.27) rather than being uniformly zero, i.e. it is per-request and degrades progressively, not a single hard break. ## Ruled out - **Draft weight loading / quantization.** `speculative_draft_model_quantization` resolves to `modelopt_fp4` while the checkpoint's `quantization_config.ignore` lists `mtp.*`. This is identical in the healthy-at-boot run, so it is not the cause. Draft loads as `Qwen4ExpForCausalLMMTP`, draft decode/extend CUDA graphs capture normally. - **Thinking mode.** `enable_thinking: true` and `false` degrade equally. - **Load/contention.** Degraded numbers reproduce at `#running-req: 1`. ## Suspected cause: #35821, and it appears absent from the image We believe this is the ghost-node path fixed by [#35821](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35821) (commit `23e51dd`, merged 2026-08-21, ported from #30451), which describes exactly the accumulate-over-time mechanism we observe: an empty node inserted with `key_len=0` becoming a stale mamba copy-on-write source that poisons later `match_prefix` calls. **The trigger named in that PR's own comment matches our workload rate.** The comment identifies the condition as `cache_finished_req` of a *short request with no track boundary*. We run `--mamba-track-interval 64`, so any request that never crosses a 64-token boundary qualifies - and our deployment produces those on a fixed schedule: a health-check chat completion every 2 minutes (~720/day) from the service watchdog, plus short agent turns. A roughly constant rate of ghost-node insertion, cleared only by a restart, is exactly the ~24 h decay and the clean restart recovery we measured. This also gives a testable prediction we have not yet run: a deployment with **no short requests** should decay far more slowly, or not at all. ### Neither half of #35821 appears to be present In `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` (digest `sha256:12d3392b…`, built 2026-08-26, `sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gd91c3682b`): - `srt/speculative/spec_utils.py` computes `to_track_ith = torch.clamp(tracking_point - seq_lens_pre_verify - 1, min=0)` - the lower bound only. The `torch.minimum(..., accept_lens - 1)` upper bound is absent; there is no `torch.minimum` anywhere in the file. - `srt/mem_cache/mamba_radix_cache.py` has `if cache_len is None:` at the patched site (line 578) without the `or cache_len == 0` branch, so it still falls through and inserts the empty node rather than freeing slots and returning. The day-0 `qwen38flashnext` image branch therefore appears to have been cut without fixes that merged to main five days before the image was built. ### A second, structurally identical clamp site that #35821 does not patch In this image, the unbounded `to_track_ith` computation appears **twice** in `spec_utils.py`: - line ~834 in `_verify_commit_step_indices()` — variables `seq_lens_pre_verify`, `mamba_track_interval`. This is the site #35821 patches. - line ~1006 in `commit_mamba_states_after_verify()` - the same computation under different names: ```python seq_pre = batch.seq_lens seq_post = batch.seq_lens + accept_lens to_track_mask = seq_pre // ti != seq_post // ti tracking_point = seq_post // ti * ti to_track_ith = torch.clamp(tracking_point - seq_pre - 1, min=0).to(torch.int64) candidate = accept_index[req_idx, to_track_ith] - accept_indices_offset ``` `accept_lens` is already a parameter of that function, so the same `torch.minimum(..., accept_lens - 1)` bound applies directly. Applying only the upstream hunk would leave this path unbounded - a partial fix that could appear to work for a while. Discussion [#36891](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/36891) describes commit `23e51dd` as "adapting merged PR #35821 … bounding accepted-state tracking across Pennyroyal's eager, fused CUDA, and KDA paths", which reads like this same multi-path issue was already encountered downstream. ## Questions for maintainers 1. Is this the same root cause as #35821, or a separate uptime-decay path specific to `qwen4_exp`? 2. Does `23e51dd` bound **both** clamp sites? If so, taking that commit wholesale looks safer than hand-porting #35821 into this branch. 3. Can the `qwen38flashnext` image be rebuilt on top of those fixes? ## Current mitigation Operational only: probe the decode log's `accept rate` every 6 h and restart both ranks when it falls below 0.35. That reliably restores 16.4 → 47.1 tok/s, but costs ~9-10 min offline per cycle (the model is a primary serving path here), so a real fix is strongly preferred. ## Launch args (abridged) ``` --tp-size 2 --nnodes 2 --node-rank 0 --quantization modelopt_fp4 --attention-backend flashinfer --page-size 64 --speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer --mamba-track-interval 64 --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.3 --mem-fraction-static 0.82 --chunked-prefill-size 1024 --max-running-requests 16 --context-length 262144 --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --enable-metrics ``` Also reported on the checkpoint's model page: https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4/discussions/8 ### Reproduction ## Reproducing / monitoring ```bash # acceptance distribution across the server's whole uptime docker logs | grep -oE 'accept rate: [0-9.]+' | sort | uniq -c # current state curl -s localhost:8010/metrics -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ | grep -E 'spec_accept_length|spec_accept_rate' ``` Note `--decode-log-interval` defaults to 40, so the decode log samples every 40 steps. --- ### Environment ## Environment - Model: `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (176B total / 6B active, 512 experts top-10, 48 layers, GDN:QSA 3:1, MTP 1 layer, 262144 ctx) - Hardware: 2× NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, **SM121**), TP=2 across nodes over ConnectX-7 RoCE - Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` @ `sha256:12d3392b…`, `sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gd91c3682b` **Disclosure:** we run a local derivative of this image that swaps the QSA packed-varlen attention for a Triton FlashDecoding-style fallback, because the stock image's flash-attn-4 CuTe-DLS kernels fail MLIR compilation on SM121. That patch touches the attention path, not the mamba radix cache or `spec_utils`. We can retest on the stock image if the QSA path is suspected, though it does not boot here unpatched.

items.title: [Bug] A non-object entry in a tool-call array discards the valid calls beside it
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When a tool-call array contains an entry that is valid JSON but not an object, the valid tool calls beside it are silently discarded.

```
[{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}, "junk"]
  -> no tool calls at all, though the first entry is a well-formed call
```

The model asked for the weather correctly; that request is lost because an unrelated entry sat next to it in the array. No crafted input is needed — only a model emitting a slightly malformed array, which is ordinary behaviour.

### Cause

`BaseFormatDetector.parse_base_json` reads `act.get("name")` without checking that `act` is an object (`python/sglang/srt/function_call/base_format_detector.py:83`):

```python
results = []
for act in action:
    name = act.get("name")
```

A non-object entry raises `AttributeError`:

```
[1, 2]   -> AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'
["x"]    -> AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'
[null]   -> AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'
[[]]     -> AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'
```

On the chat path `serving_chat.py:2145` catches that and returns `ToolCallProcessingResult(None, ...)`, dropping every call in the response.

This looks like a missed branch rather than absent error handling: the same function already defines what to do with an unusable entry a few lines below, and it is not "abort the batch" —

```python
if not (name and name in tool_indices):
    logger.warning(f"Model attempted to call undefined function: {name}")
    if not envs.SGLANG_FORWARD_UNKNOWN_TOOLS.get():
        continue  # skip this entry, keep the rest
```

An unknown tool name is skipped and parsing continues. A non-object entry should behave the same way.

### Secondary: `/parse_function_call` returns HTTP 500

The same `AttributeError` reaches the HTTP layer uncaught. `/parse_function_call` (`http_server.py:1632`) passes `obj.text` straight from the request body to `parse_non_stream` with no `try/except` — unlike `/abort_request` above it. `parse_non_stream` (`function_call_parser.py:138`) has no guard either, and the only registered exception handlers are for `HTTPException` and `RequestValidationError`, so it reaches Starlette's default handler.

That half is arguably just error handling — the input is malformed and rejecting it is correct. It is included because it is the quickest way to observe the exception, and because a 500 is the wrong way to reject a well-formed request.

### Scope

Reproduced through `FunctionCallParser.parse_non_stream()` for `qwen25`, `llama3`, `mistral` and `trinity`. Detectors with their own `try/except` (e.g. `hermes`, `deepseekv3`) are unaffected.

The discarded-valid-call effect applies to parsers whose payload between the markers is itself a JSON array (`qwen25`, `trinity`). `llama3` separates calls with `;` and mistral's `[` is part of its `bot_token`, so neither accepts an array there — for those two the uncaught exception is the only effect.

---


### Reproduction



```python
from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import Function, Tool
from sglang.srt.function_call.function_call_parser import FunctionCallParser

tools = [Tool(type="function", function=Function(
    name="get_weather", parameters={"type": "object", "properties": {}}))]

parser = FunctionCallParser(tools=tools, tool_call_parser="qwen25")

# the valid call is lost because of the entry beside it
parser.parse_non_stream(
    '<tool_call>\n[{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}, "junk"]\n</tool_call>'
)
# AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'

# minimal form
parser.parse_non_stream('<tool_call>\n[1, 2]\n</tool_call>')
# AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'
```

Against a running server:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:30000/parse_function_call \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"text": "<tool_call>\n[1, 2]\n</tool_call>",
       "tool_call_parser": "qwen25",
       "tools": [{"type": "function",
                  "function": {"name": "get_weather",
                               "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}}}]}'
```

### Environment



```
Python: 3.10.12 (main, Jul 15 2026, 23:40:17) [GCC 11.4.0]
CUDA available: True
```

items.title: [Bug] /v1/responses silently drops prompt_cache_key instead of applying it to radix-cache identity
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues and pull requests for `prompt_cache_key`, `ResponsesRequest`, and `cache_salt`.
- [x] This reproduces in the pinned development build described below.
- [x] A minimal schema-level reproduction and end-to-end measurements are included.

### Describe the bug

The OpenAI Responses API defines `prompt_cache_key` as a stable caller-provided key for prompt caching. SGLang's `ResponsesRequest` declares its native `cache_salt`, but does not declare `prompt_cache_key`.

Because the Pydantic model ignores unknown fields, an OpenAI-compatible client can send `prompt_cache_key` successfully, but the value is silently discarded. The Responses adapter then creates `GenerateReqInput` with `cache_salt=None`, so requests from distinct caller cache keys all enter the global radix-cache namespace.

This is particularly visible with agent clients. Codex sends one stable `prompt_cache_key` equal to its task/thread ID on every tool turn, and a different key for every new task. The key is present on the wire but is currently not propagated into SGLang's cache identity.

Related prior work:

- #9163 requested secure cache salting.
- #10718 added the native `cache_salt` field, including to `ResponsesRequest`.
- The missing part appears to be compatibility with the standard Responses `prompt_cache_key` field.

### Minimal schema-level reproduction

```python
from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import ResponsesRequest

request = ResponsesRequest(
    input="hello",
    prompt_cache_key="task-a",
)

# Current behavior:
assert request.cache_salt is None
assert "prompt_cache_key" not in request.model_dump()
```

The request is accepted, but the key is gone after validation.

### End-to-end observation

We captured two HTTP requests from one Codex task and two from a second task:

- Both requests within task A sent the same `prompt_cache_key`.
- Both requests within task B sent another stable `prompt_cache_key`.
- A and B had distinct keys.
- In unmodified SGLang, the parsed request still had no cache salt.

A local compatibility patch that accepts `prompt_cache_key` and uses it when `cache_salt` is absent produced the expected A/A/B/B behavior with an identical 36,022-token prompt:

| Request | Elapsed |
|---|---:|
| A, first request (cold) | 13.0247 s |
| A, second request (warm) | 0.6385 s |
| B, first request (isolated cold) | 11.9785 s |
| B, second request (warm) | 0.2287 s |

This proves same-key reuse while preventing a different caller key from matching the first namespace.

The patched deployment also completed:

- 20/20 isolated Codex agent tasks without a hang, state-leak marker, or semantically off-topic final.
- A ten-tool writable agent workflow with growing cached prefixes.

Before adding the namespace bridge, a global-cache test passed only 19/20 semantic-isolation runs, and an earlier `extra_buffer_lazy` configuration produced a fresh task that mentioned the exact path and task ID of an older task. Those observations motivated isolation, but this report does **not** claim that the missing field alone proves the separate hybrid-state corruption mechanism.

### Expected behavior

SGLang should not silently discard `prompt_cache_key`.

One possible implementation is:

```python
class ResponsesRequest(BaseModel):
    # ...
    prompt_cache_key: Optional[str] = None
```

and when creating `GenerateReqInput`:

```python
cache_salt=request.cache_salt or request.prompt_cache_key
```

This preserves an explicitly supplied native `cache_salt` while making standard Responses clients cache-aware without SGLang-specific request fields.

If `prompt_cache_key` is intentionally not equivalent to a hard cache namespace, it should still be accepted and given defined/documented cache-affinity semantics rather than silently ignored.

### Environment

- SGLang: `0.0.0.dev1+ga1fe4e30a`
- Base image digest: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-pinned@sha256:5d8382c65d1e1a7905a4852558e4e13872fa8d12312f36db04dcc9b1c7313299`
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 5090 32 GB
- Model family: Qwen3.8-27B hybrid GDN
- Radix cache: enabled
- Mamba radix strategy: `no_buffer`
- Overlap scheduler: disabled, as required by cache-enabled `no_buffer`
- Maximum running requests: 1
- API: `POST /v1/responses`

items.title: [Bug] GPT-OSS with DP attention enabled produces garbage output (GSM8K 0/128 vs 124/128)
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

## Describe the bug

Enabling `--enable-dp-attention` on GPT-OSS-120B (MXFP4) with `--tp 4 --dp 4 --ep 4 --moe-a2a-backend none` completely breaks generation, while the identical command without DP attention works fine.

With DP attention on, responses are dominated by repeated Harmony channel markers, empty final answers, and runaway generation that hits the 8192-token cap. Fixed-prompt evals (temperature 0, seed 4242):

| | GSM8K (first 128, 5-shot) | MMLU (fixed 128 subset) |
|---|---|---|
| DP attention off | 124/128 (96.9%) | 110/128 (85.9%) |
| DP attention on | **0/128 (0%)** | **4/128 (3.1%)** |

The problem is not specific to chunk size, MoE runner backend (`flashinfer_mxfp4` or `triton`), CUDA graph, overlap schedule, radix cache, or hybrid SWA KV pool — we tried toggling each one alone and none recovered basic QA. Also reproducible on current `main` by source inspection; the GPU repro below was on v0.5.18.



### Reproduction

Official image `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18`, model `openai/gpt-oss-120b`:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path openai/gpt-oss-120b \
  --tp 4 --dp 4 --ep 4 --moe-a2a-backend none \
  --quantization mxfp4 --dtype bfloat16 \
  --attention-backend trtllm_mha --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --max-total-tokens 1048576 --max-prefill-tokens 131072 \
  --context-length 65536 --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --disable-flashinfer-autotune \
  --random-seed 4242 --cuda-graph-max-bs 128 --max-running-requests 512 \
  --disable-radix-cache --reasoning-parser gpt-oss --tool-call-parser gpt-oss \
  --chunked-prefill-size 65536 --enable-dp-attention
```

The control (working) run is the same command with `--dp 4 --enable-dp-attention` removed and `--chunked-prefill-size 16384` (both land at an effective chunk of 16384 per rank). Eval via the OpenAI-compatible API with temperature 0, top_p 1, seed 4242, `reasoning_effort=low`, max_tokens 8192, concurrency 128; ask something trivial like "What is 2+2? Reply with only the number." — the DP-attention server returns channel-marker gibberish or an empty final answer.


### Environment


Run inside the official Docker image `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18` (ARM64, index digest `sha256:e42d0524...`), so the image itself pins the environment:

- sglang 0.5.18 (launch_server reports v0.5.18; container source matches the `v0.5.18` tag, commit `71de97b2`)
- PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, FlashInfer 0.6.17, Transformers 5.12.1, Triton 3.7.1, numpy 2.3.5
- 4× NVIDIA GB200 (185 GiB visible per GPU), driver 580.95.05
